as_told.title: Condon report and AARO still leave over 30% unidentified

tellings.quote: Our general conclusion is that nothing has come from the study of UFOs in the past 21 years that has added to scientific knowledge.

It is our impression that the defense function could be performed within the framework established for intelligence and surveillance operations without the continuance of a special unit such as Project Blue Book, but this is a question for defense specialists rather than research scientists.
On December 17, 1969, the Secretary of the Air Force announced the termination of Project BLUE BOOK, the Air Force program for the investigation of UFOS.

The decision to discontinue UFO investigations was based on an evaluation of a report prepared by the University of Colorado entitled, "Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects;" a review of the University of Colorado's report by the National Academy of Sciences; past UFO studies and Air Force experience investigating UFO reports during the 40s, '50s, and '60s.

plain: The Condon report, a University of Colorado study of UFO reports led by Edward Condon and dated 31 October 1968, is said to have ended Project Blue Book, the US Air Force's UFO study of the 1950s and 60s. Michels tells it himself several times: the report "closed shop on Bluebook" and explained away many cases in ordinary terms. Yet he says that if you read the substance, "over 30% of cases were totally still unidentified", a point he credits to J. Allen Hynek, an astronomer who worked on the Air Force project. He compares that with AARO, the Pentagon's present UFO office, which under its director Sean Kirkpatrick also left cases unexplained. The report's own conclusion is that "nothing has come from the study of UFOs in the past 21 years that has added to scientific knowledge". On closing Blue Book it gives only Condon's "impression" that the defense role could be done without "a special unit such as Project Blue Book", calling that "a question for defense specialists", so the report recommends and leaves the decision to others. An Air Force fact sheet of January 1985 says the Secretary of the Air Force ended Blue Book on December 17, 1969, based on "an evaluation" of the Colorado report and other reviews. Michels does not say where the report gives the share of over 30%, and the edition read here states no overall figure for unidentified cases, so the number is his reading of the cases rather than a line in the text.

discussion.by: Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects (the Condon report, 1968)
discussion.text: The report, sent to the Air Force on 31 October 1968, did not itself close Blue Book: Condon gives as his "impression" that the defense function could be performed without "a special unit such as Project Blue Book" and calls that "a question for defense specialists". The tellers do not say where the report gives "over 30%" of cases as unidentified; the report's text read here (the NCAS edition) states no overall share of unidentified cases.
